newsitem.title: INDIA: India NSE plans to target Middle East markets.
newsitem.headline: India NSE plans to target Middle East markets.

text.p: India's National Stock Exchange (NSE), has set its sights on the Middle East, after having revolutionised the country's stockmarket trading, bourse chief R.H. Patil said on Wednesday.
India's strict exchange control regulations are the only hurdle in the NSE's path, Patil told a news conference.
Plans to go overseas would depend on when the federal government decided to permit convertibility of the rupee on the capital account, Patil said.

"But in the meantime we are working out the exchange control implications of providing trading terminals in the Middle East," he said. "Orders and trades will come from there, but settlements will be done in India."
Patil said the NSE, India's first on-line exchange, executed an average of 150,000 trades each day, compared to 1,000 trades daily when it was first set up in April 1993.

"The NSE is the best, most transparent, most efficiently managed and investor friendly exchange," Patil said. "The spread between buy and sell figures has come down by a factor of 20 or 30, and this is what the NSE has done all over the country."
The NSE's operations are streamlined compared to the lengthy delays that bedevil the functioning of most of India's 23 stock exchanges, Patil said.

One hundred and four Indian cities have been linked to the NSE's very small aperture terminal (VSAT) network, taking trading opportunities out of the big commercial centres for the first time, he added.
"We are taking the exchange to the door of the investor," Patil said. "Of the 104 cities, 85 did not know what an exchange is." He said the NSE wanted to expand still further.

"By the end of December we want to be in 200 cities," he said. "As an experiment, the NSE has succeeded. We wanted to develop the concept of an exchange as a utility rather than an entity owned by the brokers."

To fuel its growth, Patil said the NSE planned to exploit two or three important features of emerging trends in India's debt and equity markets, revitalised by a five-year-old programme of free market reforms.
Investment in India's crumbling infrastructure sector, which has emerged as the chief bottleneck to reform, will have a large debt component, he predicted.

"In the smaller places there is still a tremendous attraction for debt instruments," Patil said. "Over the next few years, tax benefits and attractive rates of return will attract people to these projects."
The NSE is working on a retail debt market screen, which is in an advanced stage of preparation and would be ready within the next couple of months, Patil added.
"We are also working on the settlement software. By the end of the year, we hope to start a retail debt market."
